title: Mega Backdoor Roth: $72,000 a Year
subtitle: Most people know the $7,500 Roth IRA. Few know about the after-tax 401(k) trick that can shovel up to $72,000 a year into Roth.
source_irs: IRC §402(c)(2); IRC §415(c); SECURE Act 2.0 §603 (Roth employer match)

concepts.heading: What It Is
concepts.lede: An after-tax 401(k) contribution, then in-plan conversion to Roth. Up to $72,000 a year into Roth — not $7,500.
body: Three pieces have to line up: 1) your 401(k) plan must allow after-tax contributions, 2) it must allow in-plan Roth conversions, 3) it must allow in-service distributions or in-plan rollovers.
The combined 2025 §415(c) limit is $72,000 (employee + employer + after-tax).
About 70% of large 401(k) plans support the mega backdoor. Most small plans don't.

concepts.heading: The $72,000 Math
concepts.lede: Stack the components. Every dollar that flows through ends up in Roth.
body: Employee deferral: $24,500 (2026) — goes to traditional 401(k) pre-tax.
After-tax contribution: the remainder, up to the $72,000 §415(c) cap.
Convert the after-tax dollars to Roth. Earnings on the after-tax dollars get pro-rated.

concepts.heading: How to Start
concepts.lede: Ask HR three questions. If yes, yes, and yes — fund it.
body: 1. Does our 401(k) plan allow after-tax contributions?
2. Can I do an in-plan Roth conversion?
3. Is there an automatic conversion feature?
If yes to all three: contribute the max, then convert the after-tax slice weekly to minimize earnings.
